title: How Much Does Google Ads Advertising Cost in Serbia?
seoTitle: How Much Does Google Ads Cost in Serbia? | Tyne Agency
excerpt: How much does Google Ads cost in Serbia? Find out what budget you need, how much a click costs, what campaign management costs, and how to set a budget for your business.
keywords: how much does Google Ads cost in Serbia, Google Ads price, Google Ads price Serbia, Google Ads budget, cost of a Google Ads campaign, Google Ads agency cost, how much does Google advertising cost, Google Ads CPC Serbia, Google Ads advertising Serbia, cost of managing Google Ads campaigns
html:
Google Ads is one of the most common ways for companies to reach customers at the exact moment they're actively searching for a product or service. But one of the first questions business owners ask is: how much does Google Ads advertising actually cost in Serbia?

The short answer is: there's no single fixed price. You could spend a few hundred euros a month, a few thousand, or significantly more. The cost depends on the industry, competition, keywords, campaign goals, geographic area, ad and landing page quality, and how well the campaign is set up and optimized.

It's important to distinguish between the advertising budget and the cost of managing Google Ads campaigns.

How much does Google Ads cost in Serbia?

Google Ads doesn't have a standard price list where a single ad costs a fixed amount.

Google uses an auction system. When a user runs a search that can trigger an ad, advertisers compete for position, and the price depends on competition and other factors that affect the auction. Ad relevance and landing page experience quality also matter.

That's why the cost of a single click can vary significantly from one industry to another. A click for a highly competitive service can cost many times more than a click for a product or service with less competition.

So it's not enough to ask "How much does Google Ads cost?" A much more useful question is: "How much do I need to spend to get enough quality clicks and conversions?"

What does the cost of Google Ads advertising consist of?

  1. Advertising budget — the money spent directly on Google Ads campaigns.
  2. Managing Google Ads campaigns — strategy, keyword research, campaign structure, ads, bidding, optimization, testing, analysis, and reporting.

In the Serbian market, there are different pricing models — from a fixed monthly fee, to a percentage of the budget, to a combination of a fixed fee and a percentage. There's no universal market price list.

Your Google Ads budget isn't the same as the management fee

If a company has a total monthly budget of €700, that doesn't mean all €700 goes to Google.

For example, €500 might be the Google Ads budget, and €200 the fee for managing the campaigns. The actual media investment is then €500.

That's why you should always ask how much money actually goes to Google Ads, and how much is the management fee.

What Google Ads budget do you need in Serbia?

There's no single minimum budget that fits every company.

More important than "how much can I spend?" is the question "how much do I need to spend to get enough data and conversions to make decisions?"

Budget examples

€200–300 per month

Can make sense for a small local business, testing a single service, a very narrow geographic area, or a small number of keywords.

A budget like this can be limiting if CPC is high or if the business has a large number of products and services.

€300–500 per month

This can be a starting budget for local services, certain B2B services, specialized services, smaller online stores, and narrowly targeted Search campaigns.

The advantage is having more room to test and gather data.

€500–1,000 per month

For many small and mid-sized businesses, this is a more practical level of investment. It can leave more room for keyword groups, different ads, landing pages, locations or services, and remarketing.

€1,000–2,500 per month

This budget level already allows for a more serious approach to campaigns. Depending on the business, you can work on a larger number of Search campaigns, Performance Max campaigns, e-commerce campaigns, remarketing, and testing different offers.

€2,500+ per month

For larger companies and online stores, budgets can be many times higher. At this point, the focus shifts from just the number of clicks to profitably scaling acquisition.

This requires tracking revenue, ROAS, CAC, margin, products, and conversion quality.

How much does one click cost on Google?

There's no single click price for Serbia. The cost depends on the specific auction and keyword.

You can have one keyword with a CPC of a few cents and another with a CPC of several times that, even within the same account.

That's why average CPC on its own doesn't tell you enough.

Is a cheaper CPC always better?

No.

Imagine two campaigns. Campaign A has a CPC of €0.25, 100 clicks, and zero purchases. Campaign B has a CPC of €0.85, 100 clicks, and 10 sales.

Even though the second campaign had a more expensive click, it can be far more valuable to the business.

That's why Google Ads shouldn't be optimized just for CPC, CTR, and click count, but for actual business results.

What matters more than CPC?

  • Conversion Rate — the percentage of users who take the desired action.
  • CPA — the average cost of a single conversion.
  • ROAS — revenue relative to the advertising budget spent.
  • CAC — the cost of acquiring a new customer.
  • Profit — whether the campaign contributes to the business after all costs.

A good Google Ads campaign should generate relevant traffic and conversions, not just clicks.

What budget do you actually need?

One of the best ways to determine your budget is to start from your business economics.

For example, if the average sale value is €100, gross margin is €40, and the maximum acceptable acquisition cost is €20, the budget should be viewed through the relationship CPC → Conversion Rate → CPA → revenue → margin → profit.

If the conversion rate is 2%, you need roughly 50 clicks for one conversion. At a CPC of €0.50, that's about €25 for that traffic; at a CPC of €1, about €50.

Google Ads budget for a local business

Local businesses often don't need a large budget to get started. A plumber, dental practice, auto repair shop, law firm, beauty salon, private clinic, or accounting agency can target a specific city or part of a city.

Geographic targeting, relevant keywords, and a quality landing page can matter more than simply increasing the budget.

Google Ads budget for an online store

An online store can have hundreds or thousands of products, different categories, margins, and average order values.

The strategy can include Search, Shopping where available and appropriate, Performance Max, remarketing, brand campaigns, and campaigns by category or product.

It's important to know how much revenue a campaign generates and how much profit remains after advertising costs.

Does a bigger Google Ads budget mean more sales?

Not automatically.

If a campaign spends €500 and achieves good results, increasing it to €2,000 doesn't automatically mean four times more sales.

Demand isn't infinite. Before increasing your budget, you should check whether there's additional relevant demand you can actually capture.

What if I have a small budget?

A small budget doesn't automatically mean Google Ads makes no sense, but it does mean you need to be more selective.

Instead of advertising many products, services, and an entire country, it may make more sense to start with your single most profitable service, one location, and the most relevant keywords.

How much does a Google Ads agency cost in Serbia?

The cost of management depends on account size, number of campaigns, products, markets, tracking complexity, required level of optimization, and reporting scope.

There are fixed monthly fees, a percentage of the advertising budget, and combined models.

Most importantly, the client should know exactly what they're getting for the fee and how much money actually goes toward advertising.

How much does Google Ads management cost at Tyne Agency?

At Tyne Agency, Google Ads management starts from €299 per month + 10% of the advertising budget, depending on the scope of work and the needs of the specific business.

The fee can include analysis and strategy, campaign structure, keyword research, setup, writing and testing ads, optimization, bidding, results analysis, and monthly reporting.

For companies that need a Google + Meta approach, Tyne also offers a package covering both platforms.

The goal isn't just to spend the budget, but to connect campaigns to real business goals.

Should you hire a Google Ads agency right away?

Not every business needs to hire an agency immediately.

If you have a simple business, a small number of products or services, enough time to learn, and a basic understanding of Google Ads, you can start on your own.

Complexity grows quickly once you have multiple campaigns, a larger budget, e-commerce, more products, more locations, serious conversion tracking, GA4, GTM, a CRM, or a need to scale.

Don't start with the question "How much should I spend?"

  1. Define the goal — sales, leads, calls, bookings, or visits.
  2. Calculate the economics — what's a new customer worth to you, what CAC can you accept, and what's your margin.
  3. Research demand — how many people are searching for your products or services.
  4. Research competition — how competitive the market is.
  5. Set up tracking — without quality conversion tracking, it's hard to know if a campaign is working.
  6. Only then set the budget — the budget should be a result of strategy, not a randomly chosen number.

Is Google Ads worth it?

Google Ads can be a very valuable channel when there's relevant demand and the campaign is set up properly.

Its big advantage is that you can reach a user at the exact moment they're actively searching for what you offer.

Google Ads isn't a machine where you put in €500 and automatically get a certain number of sales. The result depends on demand, offer, keywords, ads, landing page, tracking, optimization, and business economics. For more detail on how Google Ads works, see our article Google Ads: What It Is, How It Works, and How It Drives Business Growth.

Conclusion: how much money should you set aside for Google Ads?

There's no universal answer.

For some local businesses, a few hundred euros a month can be enough to get started. For e-commerce or competitive industries, it may take significantly more.

The most important thing is to separate the Google Ads budget from the campaign management fee and look at what you're actually getting for that money.

Instead of "How much does a click cost?", it's more useful to ask: "How much does a new customer cost me, and how much does that customer bring in?" That's the difference between plain advertising and performance marketing.

If you're not sure whether Google Ads or Meta Ads is the better choice for your business, read our article Google Ads or Meta Ads: Which Channel Is Better for Your Business? as well.

Want to find out how much sense Google Ads makes for your business?

At Tyne Agency, we don't start from a predefined budget.

We first analyze your business, offer, market, competition, potential demand, current campaigns, tracking, and acquisition economics, and then define a strategy and budget that make sense for your specific goal.

title: Google Ads or Meta Ads: Which Channel Is Better for Your Business?
seoTitle: Google Ads or Meta Ads: Which Channel to Choose?
excerpt: Learn the differences between Google Ads and Meta Ads, when each channel makes more sense, and how to choose the right strategy for your business.
keywords: Google Ads or Meta Ads, difference between Google Ads and Meta Ads, which channel is better, Google Ads vs Meta Ads, performance marketing channels, Google Ads for local business, Meta Ads for e-commerce, choosing a marketing channel, Google and Meta together, digital marketing strategy
html:
Google Ads or Meta Ads? This is one of the most common questions business owners ask when they want to invest money in online advertising.

The answer isn't simple — there's no universally better channel. Google Ads and Meta Ads work on different principles and can play completely different roles in a marketing strategy.

Google most often catches users who already have a need and are actively searching for a solution, while Meta lets you introduce a product or service to people who may not yet be actively looking for what you offer.

That's why the right choice depends on your product or service, target audience, sales process, budget, and campaign goal.

Below we explain the differences between Google Ads and Meta Ads advertising, when each channel makes the most sense, and how to assess what fits your business.

Google Ads: Advertising when the user is already looking for a solution

Google Ads is especially interesting when people already use Google to find the product or service they want.

For example, someone who needs a plumber might search:

  • "plumber near me"
  • "emergency plumber"
  • "plumber London"

Someone who wants to buy a specific product might search:

  • "Kärcher vacuum price"
  • "floor washing machine"
  • "garden tools price"

In these situations, the user is already showing a certain level of purchase intent.

Google Ads lets a business appear at the exact moment a potential customer is looking for what the company offers.

When can Google Ads make particular sense?

  • local services
  • e-commerce stores
  • professional services
  • B2B services with clear search intent
  • travel and transport services
  • certain health and aesthetic services, in line with advertising rules
  • products and services people actively search for

One of the biggest advantages of Google Ads is precisely this search intent.

A user searching "estate lawyer near me" is in a completely different stage of the process than someone who simply sees an Instagram ad for a law firm.

Meta Ads: When you want to reach potential customers

Meta Ads — advertising on Facebook and Instagram — works differently.

Users usually don't open Instagram because they want to buy a specific product. They opened the app to look at content, communicate, or do something else.

That's why Meta can be especially useful when you need to: capture attention → introduce a product/service → build interest → drive action.

For example, a cosmetics brand can use video to show a product, results of use, application method, or customer experience.

A restaurant can showcase new dishes.

A fitness business can show transformations and workouts.

An e-commerce brand can test different products, offers, and creative formats.

When can Meta Ads be a good choice?

Meta is especially interesting for businesses where visual presentation, creative content, and audience interest play a big role.

  • beauty and cosmetics
  • fashion
  • fitness
  • restaurants and food
  • lifestyle products
  • e-commerce
  • education and courses
  • certain local services
  • brands that want to build recognition

A big advantage of Meta is the ability to test different creatives, messages, offers, and formats.

Google Ads vs Meta Ads — the key difference

The simplest way to present the difference:

Google Ads Meta Ads
Captures existing demand Creates and builds interest
User is actively searching User discovers a product/service
Search intent is very important Creative and messaging are very important
Text ads are key on Search Video, images, and UGC play a big role
Great for high-intent searches Great for discovery and demand generation
Search, Shopping, Performance Max, etc. Facebook, Instagram, and various Meta formats
Can be very effective for local services Can be very effective for visual products

However, this isn't a strict divide.

Google Ads can build demand through certain formats, and Meta Ads can generate direct sales and leads.

That's why a channel should be viewed in the context of the specific business, rather than through the simple rule "Google is for sales, Meta is for awareness."

What's better for e-commerce?

For online stores, both channels often make sense, but for different reasons.

Say you sell home appliances. On Google, you can target people who are already searching for specific products, categories, or models.

On Meta, you can present products through:

  • video demonstrations
  • UGC
  • lifestyle photography
  • promotions
  • new products
  • bundle offers
  • remarketing

Google can catch a user who already knows what they want. Meta can introduce a product to someone who may not yet have thought about buying.

Because of that, the combination can create a broader customer journey.

What's better for a local business?

For local services, Google Ads often has a very clear advantage when there's enough relevant search volume.

"plumber near me", "auto repair shop", "dentist near me" — the user already has a specific need. Google Search lets your ad appear at the exact moment that need exists.

Meta, on the other hand, can be useful for:

  • promoting a special offer
  • building local recognition
  • video content
  • remarketing
  • lead generation

That's why, for a local business, the choice shouldn't be based only on which platform is "more popular," but on how people actually arrive at a purchase decision.

And what's better for B2B?

For B2B businesses, the answer depends on the type of product and customer.

If people are actively searching for a specific solution, Google Search can be very relevant — for example "ERP software UK", "accounting software for businesses", or "B2B marketing agency".

Meta can play a different role — especially for awareness, educational content, remarketing, and re-engaging people who've already had contact with the brand.

That's why, in B2B, it's especially important to understand the length of the sales cycle.

If a potential client takes several weeks or months to decide, it's not enough to look only at the cost of a single lead.

Google Ads or Meta Ads by business type

The table below isn't a universal rule — it's a practical framework for an initial assessment:

Business type Possible primary channel Possible secondary channel
Local services with clear demand Google Ads Meta Ads
E-commerce Google Ads + Meta Ads —
Beauty / cosmetics Meta Ads Google Ads
B2B services with clear search intent Google Ads Meta Ads
Restaurants / food Meta Ads Google Ads
Products that rely heavily on visual content Meta Ads Google Ads

What if you have a limited budget?

This is a situation where you shouldn't automatically launch both platforms.

If your budget is limited, you should first answer a few questions:

1. Are people actively searching for what you sell?

If there's strong, relevant demand, Google Search can be a logical starting point.

2. Is the product something that's easy to present visually?

If so, Meta can play a significant role.

3. What's a new customer worth?

It's not the same if one new customer brings €50 or €5,000 in revenue.

4. What's your margin?

Revenue on its own isn't enough to assess a campaign's success.

5. Do customers buy again?

For products with repeat purchases, the value of a new customer can be significantly higher than just their first purchase.

Google Ads + Meta Ads: Why combine both?

In many cases, the question isn't "Google or Meta?" but "How can Google and Meta work together?"

One possible funnel looks like this:

Meta Ads → Potential customer discovers the brand → Visits the site → Remarketing → Searches for the brand/product on Google → Google Ads → Purchase

And the reverse works too.

A user might first come through Google, look at a product, not buy anything, and later see a Meta ad.

That's why it's important to look at the whole customer journey, not just the last click.

How do you know which channel is working?

Don't focus only on:

  • number of clicks
  • cost per click
  • impressions
  • reach
  • engagement

For performance marketing, business results matter much more:

  • number of purchases
  • revenue
  • number of quality leads
  • CAC — customer acquisition cost
  • ROAS
  • conversion rate
  • average order value
  • repeat purchase rate
  • customer lifetime value

For example, a campaign generating 100 leads isn't necessarily better than one generating 30 leads.

If 15 of those 30 leads became customers, while only 5 out of the 100 did, the cost or quantity of leads alone doesn't give the full picture.

That's why data quality and properly set up conversion tracking matter a great deal.

What do we recommend before launching a campaign?

Before spending your first euro, you should define:

1. The campaign goal

Sales, quality leads, calls, bookings, sign-ups, or store visits.

2. Your target audience

Who is the ideal customer?

3. The economics

What's a new customer worth to you, and how much can you afford to pay to acquire one?

4. Tracking

Purchases, leads, calls, forms, revenue, add to cart, checkout.

5. Budget

Budget should be tied to market size, competition, business economics, and goals — not set as an arbitrary number.

So, Google Ads or Meta Ads?

There's no single answer that applies to every business.

If your potential customer is actively searching for a product or service, Google Ads can be a natural channel for capturing existing demand.

If you need to capture attention, introduce a product, test creative messages, and build interest, Meta Ads can play an important role.

If you have enough budget and the right customer journey, Google and Meta can work together, with each channel playing its own role in the funnel.

Most importantly, the choice of platform shouldn't start with the question: "Which platform is better?"

but rather: "How do our potential customers find, consider, and buy our product or service?"

The answer to that question is often the best starting point for choosing a channel.

Want to find out which channel makes more sense for your business?

At Tyne Agency, we approach Google and Meta advertising through performance marketing — from strategy and campaign setup to tracking, optimization, and business results analysis.

If you're not sure whether your business should be on Google, Meta, or both platforms, we can analyze your product, target audience, competition, and budget, and define the right approach.

Book a consultation with Tyne Agency and find out which approach makes the most sense for your business.

title: Meta Ads: What It Is, How It Works, and How It Drives Business Growth
seoTitle: Meta Ads: What It Is and How It Works
excerpt: Learn what Meta Ads is, how advertising on Facebook and Instagram works, how much it costs, which campaign types exist, and how results are measured.
keywords: Meta Ads, what is Meta Ads, how Meta Ads works, Meta advertising, Facebook advertising, Instagram advertising, Facebook Ads, Instagram Ads, Meta Ads agency, Meta Pixel, Conversions API, Meta Lead Ads, Meta Ads cost, Meta Ads budget, Meta Ads for e-commerce, Meta Ads for small businesses, ROAS Meta Ads, Meta Ads remarketing
html:
Introduction

Meta Ads is one of the most important online advertising systems, letting companies promote their products and services on platforms such as Facebook and Instagram.

Unlike Google Search ads, where users usually search actively for what they need, Meta Ads lets companies reach potential customers based on their characteristics, behavior, and previous interactions with a brand.

That makes Meta advertising especially interesting for e-commerce, services, brands, and companies that can capture attention with strong visual content.

But Meta Ads is not just "boosting an Instagram post."

Professional Meta advertising means properly defining the campaign goal, audience, creative content, budget, tracking infrastructure, and optimization process.

In this guide, we explain what Meta Ads is, how it works, which campaign types exist, how to set a budget, what the key metrics mean, and what a quality Meta Ads strategy looks like.

What is Meta Ads?

Meta Ads is Meta's advertising platform, allowing companies to show paid ads to users on Facebook, Instagram, and other Meta surfaces.

Ads can come in different formats, including photos, video, carousel, collection, Stories, Reels, feed ads, and lead forms.

The advertiser can define what they want to achieve with the campaign, who they want to reach, and how much they want to invest.

The goal can be product sales, lead generation, website visits, sign-ups, more messages, app installs, awareness, or remarketing.

How does Meta Ads work?

When you launch a Meta Ads campaign, you are not simply buying a set number of ad impressions.

Meta uses an auction system and automation to decide who will see a given ad, when they will see it, and how much the advertiser will pay for a result.

That's why simply making a good-looking ad isn't enough.

The result depends on a combination of factors: Audience + Creative + Offer + Landing Page + Conversion Tracking + Budget + Optimization.

If the audience is well defined but the ad is weak, the campaign can perform poorly. If the ad is excellent but the landing page doesn't convert, the problem may be after the click. If everything is set up well but Meta receives the wrong conversion signals, the algorithm may optimize the campaign toward the wrong users.

That's why Meta Ads should be viewed as a whole system, not just as creating ads.

Facebook and Instagram ads

Meta lets you advertise in different places across its ecosystem.

  • Facebook Feed — ads appear in the main Facebook feed.
  • Instagram Feed — ads appear among organic Instagram posts.
  • Instagram Stories — a full-screen vertical format that is especially well suited to short video ads and direct messages.
  • Instagram Reels — a video format that has become one of the key ways people consume content on Instagram.
  • Messenger and other surfaces — depending on the campaign and available options, ads can also appear on other Meta surfaces.

What goals can we achieve with Meta Ads campaigns?

Meta campaigns can have different goals, and the choice of goal should match the business goal.

For example, an e-commerce company will most often care about sales, while a local service business may care more about leads or calls.

Common goals include Sales, Leads, Traffic, Engagement, Awareness, and App promotion.

Choosing the goal matters because Meta uses that information to try to find users who are more likely to take the desired action.

Meta Ads for e-commerce

Meta Ads is especially interesting for online stores because products can be presented through visual content.

E-commerce campaigns can use product images, video demonstrations, UGC, testimonials, lifestyle creatives, promotions, bundle offers, carousel ads, and dynamic product ads.

The goal isn't just to bring a user to the site. The goal is for the user to buy the product.

That's why a properly configured Purchase event is very important.

What is the Meta Pixel?

The Meta Pixel is a tool that lets companies track certain user activities on their website and connect them with Meta advertising.

Events such as PageView, ViewContent, AddToCart, InitiateCheckout, Purchase, and Lead can be tracked.

These events can help measure campaign results and build audiences.

For example, you can create an audience of people who viewed a product but didn't buy, and then show them a remarketing ad.

Conversions API (CAPI)

Besides the Meta Pixel, there is also the Conversions API, which lets you send certain event data from your server to Meta.

CAPI can be part of a higher-quality tracking infrastructure and can be used together with the Pixel.

The goal is for Meta to receive better event data and to reduce dependence on browser-side tracking alone.

For more serious performance campaigns, especially when measuring sales matters, tracking infrastructure should be a priority.

Why is conversion tracking so important?

If a Meta campaign generates 100 leads, that may look like a great result at first glance. But after phone calls, it may turn out that a large share of those leads are low quality.

If Meta only receives the signal "100 leads," it doesn't have the same view of quality that your sales team has.

That's why, in lead generation campaigns, it's especially important to think about lead quality, not just quantity.

Meta Lead Ads

Meta lets companies run Lead Ads campaigns with forms that users can fill out directly inside the Meta platform.

This can reduce friction in the lead generation process.

A lead form can include questions that help qualify a potential client, for example "What is your monthly advertising budget?" or "Which service do you want to promote?"

This is especially useful when you want to optimize not just for the quantity of leads, but for their relevance.

How do you qualify leads?

Cost per lead isn't a sufficient metric.

Campaign A can generate 100 leads at €5 each, while Campaign B generates 30 leads at €15 each. If most leads from the first campaign are low quality and the second campaign generates real prospects, the second campaign can have greater business value.

That's why it's useful to track: Lead → Qualified Lead → Sales Opportunity → Customer.

This way, marketing and sales can work with the same data.

Meta Ads audiences

One of the big advantages of Meta advertising is the ability to work with different types of audiences.

  • Cold audience — people who haven't yet had direct interaction with your brand.
  • Warm audience — people who have already shown some interest, for example visited the site, watched a video, interacted with your Instagram profile, or clicked an ad.
  • Remarketing audience — people who have already been in contact with your brand and whom you want to reach again.
  • Custom Audiences — audiences created from available data and interactions, in line with Meta's rules.
  • Lookalike Audiences — audiences Meta creates based on the characteristics of a specific existing audience.

Advantage+ and automation

Meta is using more and more automation in advertising.

Advantage+ solutions let Meta use its own automation systems for different parts of a campaign, including audience, placements, and optimization, depending on the campaign type.

This means modern Meta advertising isn't based solely on manually picking dozens of interests.

The quality of conversion signals, creatives, and data becomes increasingly important.

That's why it's very important that Meta receives the most precise information possible about what success means for your business.

How much does Meta advertising cost?

There is no universal price for Meta ads.

Cost depends on the market, competition, target audience, ad quality, campaign goal, placement, season, offer, and landing page quality.

Some campaigns can have a very low CPC but few conversions. Others can have a more expensive click but far more quality customers.

That's why it's not a good idea to judge a campaign only by cost per click.

What is CPM?

CPM (Cost Per Mille) is the cost per 1,000 impressions.

For example, if a campaign has a CPM of €5, the average cost for 1,000 ad views is €5.

CPM can be useful for understanding the cost of reaching an audience, but on its own it doesn't tell you whether a campaign is profitable.

What is CTR?

CTR (Click-Through Rate) shows the percentage of people who clicked an ad after seeing it.

If an ad gets 10,000 impressions and 500 clicks, its CTR is 5%.

CTR can help gauge how much an ad attracts attention and how relevant it is to the audience. However, a high CTR doesn't automatically mean a high number of sales.

What is CPC?

CPC (Cost Per Click) shows the average cost of a single click.

If you spend €100 and get 200 clicks, your CPC is €0.50.

But a cheap click isn't necessarily a good click. If 200 people click and nobody buys, the campaign hasn't achieved its business goal.

What is CPA / CPL?

For campaigns that generate conversions, CPA — Cost Per Acquisition — is often tracked, meaning how much it costs to achieve a given acquisition.

For lead generation campaigns, CPL — Cost Per Lead — is often used.

For example, €300 in spend and 20 leads gives a CPL of €15.

But the real KPI may be cost per qualified lead, not just cost per lead.

What is ROAS?

For e-commerce campaigns, one of the most important metrics can be ROAS — Return on Ad Spend.

If you spend €1,000 on Meta Ads and generate €4,000 in revenue, your ROAS is 4x.

But as with Google Ads, ROAS isn't the same as profit. You need to take into account product cost, margin, shipping, discounts, operating costs, returns, and other business expenses.

Creative is one of the most important elements of a Meta Ads campaign

With Meta ads, users usually don't arrive with the intent to search for something. The ad has to interrupt the scroll and capture attention.

A good Meta creative can include a strong hook, a clear problem, a product demonstration, a benefit, social proof, UGC, a testimonial, an offer, and a clear CTA.

The goal isn't just to make a nice design. The goal is to create a creative concept that attracts the right audience and leads it toward the desired action.

Why should you test multiple creatives?

There's no guarantee that any one ad will be the best.

That's why testing is one of the important parts of a Meta Ads strategy.

We can test different hooks, video vs. image, UGC vs. branded creative, different offers, CTA messages, products, formats, and landing pages.

Based on the results, we can decide which elements to develop further.

Remarketing: how to win back interested users

Many users won't buy on their first visit to a site.

That's why remarketing can be an important part of a strategy.

A user may first see an ad, visit the site, look at a product, and not buy. Later they may see a remarketing ad, return to the site, and complete the purchase.

Remarketing can be especially useful for products or services where users need more time to make a decision.

Meta Ads and the landing page

A good ad can't fully make up for a bad landing page.

If an ad promises 20% off the first order and the user doesn't see a clear offer on the page, they may leave the site.

That's why Ad → Landing Page → Offer → CTA should be aligned.

For e-commerce in particular, pay attention to price, availability, photos, benefits, reviews, shipping, payment methods, and checkout.

Meta Ads for different types of business

  • E-commerce — Sales campaigns, product ads, remarketing, and creative testing.
  • Local services — Lead generation, calls, messages, and remarketing.
  • Beauty and wellness — Visual content, UGC, offers, testimonials, and lead generation.
  • Fitness — Transformations, educational video content, lead forms, and remarketing.
  • B2B — Awareness, remarketing, lead generation, and testing different messages for the target audience.
  • Brands — Awareness, video, engagement, community building, and long-term remarketing.

Meta Ads for small businesses

Meta Ads isn't reserved for large companies only.

A small business can start with a relatively simple campaign structure, focusing on one product, one service, or one target audience.

More important than having many campaigns is having a clear goal, a good offer, a quality creative, properly set up tracking, enough data for optimization, and realistic expectations.

With a limited budget, it's often better to test a small number of clear hypotheses than to spread the budget across many campaigns and audiences.

The most common mistakes in Meta Ads advertising

  1. Boosting posts instead of strategic advertising.
  2. Too many interests and an overcomplicated audience.
  3. A single creative.
  4. Optimizing for the wrong goal.
  5. Poor tracking.
  6. Focusing only on CPL or CPC.
  7. Ignoring the landing page.

What does a good Meta Ads strategy look like?

A good Meta Ads strategy can be viewed through a few steps:

  1. Define the goal — Sales, Leads, Calls, or Awareness.
  2. Define the ideal customer.
  3. The offer — why would a user react right now?
  4. Creative strategy — which messages, formats, and angles do we want to test?
  5. Tracking — are we properly tracking what matters to us?
  6. Campaign — set up the appropriate structure and budget.
  7. Testing — test creatives, messages, audiences, and offers.
  8. Optimization — analyze the data and redistribute budget toward what delivers better results.
  9. Scaling — once we find what works, we can gradually increase investment.

How do you measure the success of a Meta Ads campaign?

The right KPI depends on the business goal.

  • For e-commerce: Purchases, Revenue, ROAS, CAC, Conversion Rate, AOV, and Repeat Purchase Rate.
  • For lead generation: Leads, CPL, Qualified Leads, Cost per Qualified Lead, Sales Opportunities, Customers, and CAC.
  • For awareness: Reach, Impressions, CPM, Video Views, Frequency, and Brand metrics.

The most important thing is to connect marketing metrics to business results.

Meta Ads or Google Ads?

Google and Meta don't have to be competing channels.

Google Ads can catch a user who is already actively looking for a product or service. Meta Ads can introduce a product to a user who hasn't yet been actively searching for a solution.

That's why a combination can be very useful, with each channel playing its own role in the funnel.

The right choice depends on how customers find your product, how long the decision process takes, and what the economics of your business look like.

Conclusion

Meta Ads is far more than advertising on Instagram and Facebook.

A successful Meta campaign requires a combination of strategy, a quality offer, creative content, the right audience, tracking, testing, and optimization.

Most importantly, a campaign shouldn't be judged only by clicks, impressions, or leads.

The real question is: does Meta Ads bring in quality customers, and is acquiring them profitable?

When tracking and strategy are set up properly, Meta Ads can be a powerful channel for sales, lead generation, remarketing, and brand building.

At Tyne Agency, we approach Meta advertising through performance marketing — from strategy and campaign creation to the Meta Pixel, the Conversions API, creative testing, optimization, and business results analysis.

We don't focus only on how many people saw or clicked an ad. The focus is on how many quality customers or clients a campaign can bring in, and how that result can be scaled further.

title: Google Ads: What It Is, How It Works, and How It Drives Business Growth
seoTitle: Google Ads: What It Is and How It Works
excerpt: Learn what Google Ads is, how it works, what campaign types exist, how much advertising costs, and how Google Ads results are measured.
keywords: Google Ads, what is Google Ads, how Google Ads works, Google Ads advertising, Google Ads campaign, Google Ads price, Google Ads budget, Google Ads agency, Google Ads for small businesses, Google Ads for e-commerce, Google Ads tracking, ROAS Google Ads, Google Search Ads
html:
Introduction

If you've ever searched Google and noticed results labeled "Sponsored," there's a good chance you were looking at Google Ads.

Google Ads is one of the best-known online advertising platforms, letting companies put their products and services in front of potential customers at the exact moment those customers are searching for them or showing interest.

Unlike traditional advertising, where you pay to have your message seen by as many people as possible, Google Ads lets you direct your budget more precisely toward users who are already showing intent or interest.

In this guide, we cover the fundamentals of Google Ads — from your first ad to measuring results.

What is Google Ads?

Google Ads is Google's advertising platform, allowing companies to pay to promote products and services to users on Google Search and across other Google channels.

The most familiar example is Search ads. If someone searches "plumber near me," a plumbing company can appear among the paid results.

Similarly, an online store can appear when a shopper searches for a specific product, model, or category.

The main advantage of this approach is user intent: the person is already looking for something, and the advertiser tries to show up at exactly that moment.

How does Google Ads work?

The advertiser defines a campaign goal, selects products or services, defines relevant keywords and/or other signals, creates ads, sets a budget, sets up conversion measurement, and monitors results.

When a user runs a relevant search, Google evaluates which ads can be shown and in what order.

That's why simply paying more doesn't guarantee the top spot. Results are influenced by ad relevance, landing page experience quality, competition, and other factors in Google's ad auction system.

What are keywords?

For Search campaigns, keywords are one of the core elements of the strategy.

If you run an agency offering Google Ads services, relevant searches might include "google ads agency," "google ads management," and "google ads pricing."

If you run a plumbing company, relevant searches might include "plumber London," "emergency plumber," and "plumber near me."

The goal isn't to show your ad for as many searches as possible. The goal is to show it for relevant searches that have the potential to bring in the right customer.

Search campaigns: when a user is actively looking for your product or service

Google Search Ads are text ads that can appear on the Google search results page.

They're especially effective when there's clear demand for a product or service. For example, someone searching "dentist near me" already has a specific need. The same applies to "buy Kärcher vacuum" or "airport transfer."

In these situations, Google Ads lets a company be present at the exact moment a potential customer is actively looking for a solution.

Google Shopping and e-commerce

Shopping ads display products along with information such as product name, price, image, store, and other relevant details.

For an online store, the goal isn't just getting a user to visit the site. It's important to track what happens after the click: Product view → Add to cart → Checkout → Purchase.

That data makes it possible to assess which products, campaigns, and segments actually deliver results.

Performance Max campaigns

Performance Max campaigns use Google's automated systems to show ads across different Google channels, depending on the campaign goal and available data.

The system tries to find users with the highest likelihood of completing the desired conversion. This can be especially interesting for e-commerce and companies that have enough quality data to optimize against.

However, automation doesn't mean a campaign can just be launched and left unattended. Data quality, conversion tracking, campaign structure, product feed, creative assets, and business goals still matter a great deal.

Display ads

The Google Display Network shows visual ads across a wide range of websites and digital surfaces within Google's advertising ecosystem.

Display can serve different roles, including remarketing, building awareness, promoting an offer, and re-engaging users who've already visited your site.

For example, a user might visit an online store, look at a product, but not complete a purchase. Later, they might see an ad for that same brand while browsing other sites. That's one example of remarketing.

How much does Google Ads cost?

There's no universal price.

Google Ads runs on an auction system, and cost depends on many factors, including competition, industry, keywords, location, ad quality and relevance, campaign goal, market, and demand.

That's why two companies can end up with completely different costs per click even when running the same type of campaign.

It's important to distinguish between your advertising budget and the cost of managing campaigns. For example, a €1,000 monthly Google Ads budget is money spent on the platform and ad delivery itself. The cost of an agency or specialist managing the campaigns is a separate expense.

How much budget should you allocate?

Budget depends on market size, average cost per click, competition, the value of your product or service, margin, your target number of conversions, and expected acquisition cost.

A local business targeting a single city may need a completely different budget than an e-commerce company selling nationwide.

That's why budget should be viewed in the context of your business economics, not just as a fixed monthly number.

What is CPC?

CPC (Cost Per Click) is the price an advertiser pays for a click on an ad.

If you spend €100 and get 200 clicks, your CPC is €0.50.

But a low CPC on its own doesn't mean a campaign is successful. You can have very cheap clicks that never turn into a single sale. That's why CPC needs to be looked at alongside other metrics.

What is CTR?

CTR (Click-Through Rate) is the percentage of people who click an ad after seeing it.

If an ad gets 10,000 impressions and 500 clicks, its CTR is 5%.

CTR can help gauge how well an ad matches a given search or audience. However, even a high CTR doesn't guarantee a business result. If people click the ad but don't buy or submit an inquiry, you need to analyze what happens after the click.

What is a conversion?

A conversion is the desired action a user takes after interacting with an ad.

That could be a purchase, a form submission, a phone call, a booking, a sign-up, a consultation request, or a downloaded offer.

For e-commerce businesses, the main conversion will often be a purchase. For a local business, it might be a call or a submitted form.

That's why it's essential to define what a successful outcome actually means for your specific business.

What is ROAS?

ROAS — Return on Ad Spend — shows how much revenue you generate relative to what you spend on ads.

If you spend €1,000 on Google Ads and generate €5,000 in revenue, your ROAS is 5x.

But ROAS isn't the same as profit. If margins are thin, product costs are high, or there are other operating costs, a campaign with a high ROAS isn't automatically the most profitable one.

That's why ROAS should be viewed in the context of your overall business economics.

Why is conversion tracking so important?

One of the biggest mistakes in Google Ads advertising is looking only at clicks and impressions.

If you don't know what happened after the click, you can't reliably know what's actually working.

That's why conversion tracking needs to be set up correctly. Depending on the business, you might track purchases, leads, phone calls, form submissions, add-to-cart events, checkouts, revenue, and transaction value.

Tools like Google Analytics 4 (GA4) and Google Tag Manager (GTM) are often part of that tracking infrastructure. For e-commerce in particular, it's important — wherever possible — to track not just the number of purchases but the actual revenue value generated.

Google Ads isn't "set it and forget it"

A well-performing Google Ads campaign requires ongoing analysis and optimization.

That can include reviewing search terms, adding negative keywords, optimizing budget, testing ads, optimizing landing pages, analyzing conversions, refining bidding strategy, testing new keywords, reviewing traffic quality, remarketing, and analyzing results by device, location, and other segments.

The goal isn't just to spend the budget. The goal is to direct the budget toward where the business result has the greatest potential.

What mistakes do companies most often make?

  1. Not setting up conversion tracking — If you don't know what led to a sale or a lead, it's hard to optimize a campaign.
  2. Targeting overly broad searches — More clicks doesn't automatically mean more customers.
  3. Not using negative keywords — Irrelevant searches can quietly drain your budget.
  4. Sending all traffic to the homepage — The landing page should match both user intent and the ad itself.
  5. Only looking at CPC — A cheap click that doesn't lead to a result isn't necessarily a good click.
  6. Not testing ads — One ad isn't necessarily the best ad.
  7. Not connecting marketing to business results — Click and impression counts aren't enough if the goal is sales.

What does a good Google Ads strategy look like?

A good campaign starts before the first ad is even created.

The first step is understanding the business: What are you selling? Who's the customer? What are they searching for? What's a new customer worth? How much can you afford to pay for acquisition? How do you measure results? Which channel and campaign type can bring in quality traffic?

Only after that does campaign structure come into play.

Google Ads for small businesses

Google Ads isn't just for large companies.

A small business can use Google Ads too, as long as there's enough relevant demand and the campaign economics hold up.

A local service business can target just one city or a few neighborhoods. An online store can start with its most important categories and products. A professional service can target specific searches that signal high user intent.

The key isn't matching a large competitor's budget. The key is directing your budget toward relevant demand and measuring results properly.

Is Google Ads the right choice for your business?

Before launching a campaign, ask yourself a few questions:

  • Are people actively searching for my product or service?
  • What's a new customer worth to me?
  • How much can I afford to pay to acquire one?
  • Do I have a good enough landing page or web shop?
  • Can I properly track conversions?
  • Do I have enough budget for the campaign to gather sufficient data?

If the answers are positive, Google Ads can be a highly relevant channel for acquiring new customers.

Conclusion

Google Ads is far more than paid visibility on Google.

A successful campaign requires a combination of strategy, relevant demand, quality ads, a strong landing page, proper tracking, and continuous optimization.

Most importantly, Google Ads shouldn't be judged purely on click volume or cost per click.

The real question is: how many quality customers or clients is your advertising bringing in, and is acquiring them profitable?

That's exactly why Google Ads should be treated as part of a broader performance marketing system — not as an isolated channel.

Want to find out if Google Ads makes sense for your business?

At Tyne Agency, we approach Google Ads advertising end-to-end — from strategy, keyword research, and campaign setup, to conversion tracking, optimization, and business results analysis.

Book a consultation and let's work out together where the room for growth is, and how Google Ads could fit into your business.
